# Could two people in neighbouring seats hear each other before Sting took the stage?

**No. Almost certainly not.** If they stayed squarely in their seats, facing the stage, and spoke at the volume you would use in a living room, the person beside them would hear that they were talking but would not be able to make out the words. To communicate they would have to do one of the two things the question rules out: raise their voice well above conversational level, or turn and lean in so their mouth was close to the other person's ear.

## What the footage actually shows in the "before Sting" window

The clip opens with a caption reading **"Centre Bell, Montréal (Canada), Nov. 6, 2017"** — the *Tower of Song* memorial tribute concert for Leonard Cohen. Sting does not appear until roughly four and a half seconds in, when the video cross‑fades to a shot of him on stage and on the big screens and the crowd stands and applauds. Everything before that, the first ~4 seconds, is the pre‑show, and it shows the following:

- **The stage is empty and no music is being performed.** You can see the full orchestral/band rig lit in blue — rows of chairs, music stands, keyboards, a harp at stage left — but there is not a single musician sitting at them. Nobody is at a microphone.
- **The video screens are showing the static event logo**, the "Tower of Song" silhouette of Cohen in his hat, not a live camera feed. That is the classic "doors are open, show hasn't started" state.
- **The audience is still coming in and being seated.** People are standing in the aisles and shuffling along rows in winter coats and puffer jackets; the floor is packed with linked folding chairs; a young usher in a blue uniform shirt and tie is standing in the aisle with his arm outstretched, pointing people to their seats, and his mouth is open — he is calling out directions.
- **The place is essentially full.** The lower bowl behind the floor is densely occupied all the way up, and the floor seating is filled with a few people still moving to their places. The Bell Centre holds on the order of 15,000–20,000 for a concert of this kind, and the shot is consistent with a house of that size at or near capacity. Several thousand people are visible in this single camera angle alone.
- **The show is imminent but has not begun.** Atmospheric haze is already hanging in the air — that is why the blue beams over the stage read as solid shafts of light — so the rig is up and running while the room fills.

## Why that makes normal conversation impossible

1. **The dominant sound is thousands of simultaneous conversations.** The noise here is not the show — the show hasn't started. It is the crowd itself. When ten to twenty thousand people are all chatting while they file in, the aggregate babble in an arena typically sits somewhere around 75–85 dBA. On top of that, venues almost always play recorded walk‑in music over the house PA during this phase — that cannot be confirmed from a silent file, but it is the norm and it would only push the level higher. The pre‑show fill is, acoustically, one of the loudest stretches of the whole evening — often noisier than a quiet solo number later on.

2. **A normal indoor voice is well below that.** Relaxed conversational speech is roughly 55–60 dB measured a metre away. A neighbour's ear is maybe half a metre off, so perhaps the mid‑60s dB arrives. Against a 75–85 dB background that is a signal‑to‑noise ratio of about **−10 to −20 dB**. Speech intelligibility collapses once the voice falls below the background level; at −10 dB or worse you catch essentially nothing. The listener would perceive lips moving and a murmur, not sentences.

3. **The noise is the same kind of sound as the speech, which is the worst case.** Crowd babble is other people's voices, occupying exactly the frequency band speech lives in. It masks a talker far more effectively than a hum or a rumble of the same loudness would, and it offers no quiet gaps to listen through.

4. **The room itself smears whatever gets through.** An NHL arena is a huge volume of hard, reflective surfaces — concrete, steel, glass, plastic seating — with a long reverberation time and no acoustic treatment aimed at speech. Reverberation blurs consonants together, so even the fraction of a quiet voice that arrives is degraded.

5. **Their seating geometry works against them.** Everyone in the frame is in a forward‑facing row, shoulder to shoulder in narrow folding chairs. Someone speaking at normal volume without turning is projecting their voice past the *side* of their neighbour's head — off‑axis, partly shadowed by the listener's own head, and with no eye contact or visible lip movement to help. Lip‑reading and facial cues are worth several dB of effective intelligibility in noise, and facing straight ahead throws that away. Since the question specifies they do not adjust their position, they lose that help too.

6. **Everyone else is doing the same thing, which escalates it.** The Lombard effect means each person raises their voice to be heard over the others, which pushes the overall level up further. That is precisely why, in the footage, you can see people standing in clusters with their heads tipped close together, and why the usher has to project to direct patrons — the ordinary behaviour in that room is leaning in and speaking up.

## What would work instead

Anything that buys back 15–20 dB of signal‑to‑noise: turning toward the other person, leaning in until their mouth is within 10–15 cm of the listener's ear (halving the distance gains about 6 dB, and going from 50 cm to 12 cm gains around 12 dB), cupping a hand to direct the sound, raising the voice to a loud or shouting level, or simply waiting. None of those are available under the stated conditions.

## One caveat about method

The video file supplied contains a video stream only — there is no audio track — so this is an inference from what is visible rather than a measurement of the actual sound level. But the visual evidence is unambiguous about the situation: a near‑capacity arena crowd of many thousands, mid‑way through being seated, with no performance yet under way. That environment reliably produces a noise floor that swamps a normal speaking voice.

**Bottom line: no, they would not be able to hear one another. The reason is masking by crowd noise — a full ~20,000‑seat arena in its noisiest pre‑show phase, thousands of overlapping conversations in the same frequency range as speech, amplified by a long‑reverberating hard‑surfaced room and by the fact that two forward‑facing seat‑neighbours are speaking past each other rather than into each other's ear.**
